rev_cp10_h: Open doors for work other than factories and logistics, turning a “place to work” into a “place to live”
rev_cp10_p: 💡 Proposal: The city’s business-location subsidy requires at least 1,000 m² of floor space and 500 million yen of investment (100 million for SMEs), which IT, design and cultural work cannot reach. Create a small scheme measured by jobs, and workspaces in vacant homes and shops in the east, as a landing place for the settlement grant for people working in the city.
rev_cp1_h: Publish the yardsticks for learning first, and report every year
rev_cp1_p: 💡 Proposal: Before the reorganization, publish measures of attainment (such as the share of children who say they understand lessons, in a form that identifies no person or school), personal growth (such as the share who took on a role) and conditions (number of classes, grades where classes can be reshuffled, subjects with specialist teachers), and report on them every year. These can also serve as the criteria for Phase 2.
rev_cp2_h: Add teachers for the transition years
rev_cp2_p: 💡 Proposal: Use the national and prefectural extra-teacher allocations heavily in the first years after the merger, combining small-group and ability-based teaching with passing on records of where children struggle. This answers concretely the worries of year groups whose classes get bigger.
rev_cp3_h: Link nine years of inquiry learning with the district’s real issues and data
rev_cp3_p: 💡 Proposal: Take the district’s own issues — the use of closed buildings, the bus service, the population outlook — and combine lessons that graph the city’s statistics and make forecasts, projects where every child takes a role, and chances to try things with local adults. This builds maths, information skills and the ability to run a community together.
rev_cp4_h: Turn bus travel and disaster preparedness into lessons in independence and resilience
rev_cp4_p: 💡 Proposal: Hand children tasks suited to their grade, such as moving to the timetable and reporting days they will not ride. In the former school buildings kept as shelters, children, parents, the bus operator and the community draw up the disaster rules together.
rev_cp5_h: Plan health support by the number of children, not the number of schools
rev_cp5_p: 💡 Proposal: Before the new schools open, publish the number of school nurses at each, the school-doctor arrangements, and how children needing medical care will be admitted and travel by bus. Link fitness to make up for less walking, and heat measures, with health lessons.
rev_cp6_h: Publish the assumptions and targets, and make the number of children in the east a department’s goal
rev_cp6_p: 💡 Proposal: With the assumptions public, residents, businesses and the city can argue from the same figures. Put the eastern development council and the school reorganization discussions in the same forum, adopt the east’s child population as a shared indicator, and decide which department is responsible for it.
rev_cp7_h: Mix housing types as the new town changes generations
rev_cp7_p: 💡 Proposal: Review the district plan of detached houses only on plots of 150 m² or more, and turn the 166 vacant homes — the most in the city — into homes that families with children can move into, through renovation support and leasing. The prefecture and city should discuss regenerating the housing area the prefecture built within one framework.
rev_cp8_h: Treat commuting and school travel as a condition for settling
rev_cp8_p: 💡 Proposal: Children’s school buses and adults’ commutes are two sides of the same problem. In the city’s own survey, transport was among the top reasons young households gave for choosing where they moved. Consider roads and bus routes toward Kasugai and elsewhere together with housing policy.
rev_cp9_h: Make closing school sites hubs for families, and keep a high school stage as an option
rev_cp9_p: 💡 Proposal: Use the buildings nearest the district’s centre for child-rearing support, after-school places and meeting space, making up for schools being further away. Before deciding on demolition, estimate once the conditions and costs of a high school stage as an option.
rev_cp_g1: Protect and raise the quality of education
rev_cp_g2: Increase the number of children in the east
rev_cp_lead: These are this site’s proposals, not something the city is considering. The evidence for each, and what we have not been able to confirm, can be read via “More” on the In-depth page.
rev_cv10_f: 【Fact】Responsibility is split: school reorganization lies with the Board of Education, eastern development and land use with the Urban Policy Department, child-rearing with the Children’s Future Department, and business location with the Regional Revitalization Department. The Tokadai district plan and the location optimization plan are plans the city decides itself. The revised national guide asks for planning together with town development, including the mayor’s departments.
rev_cv10_h: No department has “the number of children in the east” as its goal, and the tools the city can decide on itself go unused
rev_cv10_v: 🔎 Our view: The school reorganization section deals with the result of decline; it is not there to increase numbers. In our view, the urban-planning tools that would help the east most are the ones least used.
rev_cv1_f: 【Fact】The city expects every elementary school in the district and Shinooka Junior High to have one class per grade by 2033, and says the reorganization cannot wait.
rev_cv1_h: The assumptions behind “one class per grade by 2033” are not shown
rev_cv1_v: 🔎 Our view: Only the result of the projection is published; how births, moves in and out, and new housing were assumed is not. With the assumptions, residents could separate what cannot be changed from what policy could still change.
rev_cv2_f: 【Fact】Phase 2 — merging into one elementary and one junior high school and introducing integrated elementary–junior high education — is to be considered if numbers fall further after Phase 1, judged by how Phase 1 goes.
rev_cv2_h: No criteria are given for moving on to Phase 2 (one elementary and one junior high school)
rev_cv2_v: 🔎 Our view: What level “falling further” means is not stated. Unless it is said first how Phase 1 will be measured, Phase 2 looks like a foregone conclusion.
rev_cv3_f: 【Fact】The school bus covers trips of 2 km or more plus areas chosen for local conditions, but Shiroyama 3 and 4-chome are not covered even where the district change makes the trip longer than 2 km. The usage guidelines were to be handed out at briefings, and applications ran from 30 August to 30 September 2026.
rev_cv3_h: The reasons for where the school-route lines are drawn are hard to read
rev_cv3_v: 🔎 Our view: The same 2 km can be covered in one case and not in another, and the published materials do not make the reason clear. The application deadline also came before the guidelines were settled.
rev_cv4_f: 【Fact】The use of the buildings that will close is left for future consideration in the published materials. Nationally, 74.4% of former school buildings still standing are being used for something else (MEXT survey, FY2024).
rev_cv4_h: What happens to the closed school buildings is not set out together with the closure dates
rev_cv4_v: 🔎 Our view: Schools are evacuation shelters and venues for local events. If closures go ahead before uses are decided, the area will be without that hub for a while.
rev_cv5_f: 【Fact】The public comment period drew 142 comments from 55 people. The national guide revised in August 2026 asks both for careful, two-way discussion and for a timeline that does not keep putting off a decision.
rev_cv5_h: Consensus-building is judged by how the process was designed, not by the number of comments
rev_cv5_v: 🔎 Our view: Counting comments does not measure support or opposition. What matters is how people were reached, and at which stage what could still be changed.
rev_cv6_f: 【Fact】The city says lessons where children learn from each other need a group of a certain size, and lists the problems of small schools (no class reshuffles, few chances to take on roles, and so on). The city’s appropriate size is 12–24 classes per school.
rev_cv6_h: There is no yardstick for checking whether learning and growth improve after the reorganization
rev_cv6_v: 🔎 Our view: What is shown is “the problems of today’s small schools”. We find no yardstick in the published materials for checking how attainment and personal growth change after the reorganization.
rev_cv7_f: 【Fact】The class-size cap is 35 for elementary school and the first year of junior high, and junior high is being lowered to 35 step by step until FY2027. Teacher numbers are calculated from the number of classes (Act on Standards for Class Formation and Staff Numbers). The city says it is not against small classes.
rev_cv7_h: Classes may grow: the state is making classes smaller while merging schools
rev_cv7_v: 🔎 Our view: Some year groups used to classes of just over 20 may move into classes near the cap. Here, where every grade is below 35, only the merging half of the state’s two policies has any effect. Whether extra teachers will be added for the transition years has not been said.
rev_cv8_f: 【Fact】The city sets out exchanges between schools before the merger, stronger counselling and handing on information about children who need support. School nurses are allotted basically one per school of three or more classes, and the gyms and grounds of closing schools are to stay as evacuation sites.
rev_cv8_h: Support for children’s wellbeing in the transition, and for health and safety, is not yet visible
rev_cv8_v: 🔎 Our view: Going from eight schools to four also means going from eight nurse’s offices to four. How the exchanges will be judged sufficient, bus travel and admission for children needing medical care, and preparing for the school and the home evacuation site being different are not in the published materials.
rev_cv9_f: 【Fact】Establishments in the eastern district rose from 917 in 2009 to 1,095 in 2014, and employees from 12,388 to 20,671 (Eastern District Development Strategy). Meanwhile the district’s under-20 population is less than half of what it was 20 years ago. Most of Tokadai is zoned for detached houses only, and the Tokadai Line closed in 2006.
rev_cv9_h: Jobs increased, but children did not
rev_cv9_v: 🔎 Our view: Child-rearing support that is the same anywhere in the city does little to decide which district people live in. We think the bigger factors were the lack of housing young households can move into and of ways to commute.
rev_cv_lead: From everything we have examined, we picked the 10 points that matter most for judging the plan. 【Fact】 marks what rests on published material; 🔎 marks this site’s view.

rev_deep_p: The In-depth review is in three parts. The evidence for each key point above can be read there, part by part.
rev_f10_v: Revised on 5 August 2026 for the first time in ten years. Its three pillars are wider-area, whole-of-government and modernised thinking, and it asks municipalities to consider schools together with town planning
rev_f1_v: As of 2025, the population aged 19 and under in the Shinooka district is less than half what it was 20 years ago; the population aged 65 and over is about 2.5 times larger
rev_f2_v: By 2033 every elementary school in the district, and Shinooka Junior High, is expected to have only one class per year group
rev_f3_v: In FY2027, five elementary and three junior high schools become two elementary and two junior high schools
rev_f4_v: If numbers fall further, merging into one elementary and one junior high school with integrated 9-year education is under consideration; the decision is to be made after seeing how Phase 1 goes
rev_f5_v: Held 10 November – 9 December 2025; 142 submissions from 55 people in total (submitters: 39 by e-mail, 13 by fax, 1 by post, 2 in person)
rev_f6_v: Covers children living 2 km or more from school, plus areas set with local conditions in mind. Expected users: about 100 in Tokadai Nishi and about 160 in Tokadai Higashi
rev_f7_v: Aoi Kotsu Co. won the tender at 111,750,000 yen (before tax); the contract runs from 8 June 2026 to 31 March 2030
rev_f8_v: Five councils are to become two, targeted for FY2029. How the merger will work is still to be discussed
rev_f9_v: 12 to 18 classes is the standard for elementary and junior high schools. About 40% of public elementary schools and about 50% of junior high schools nationwide are below 12 classes

rev_p: We have condensed what this site has examined into 10 key findings, and our proposals — for protecting and raising the quality of education and for increasing the number of children in the eastern district — into 10 key proposals. The evidence for each can be read in detail on the In-depth review page.

rev_s9_h: Contacts for the Departments Mentioned<small>関係する部署の問い合わせ先</small>
rev_s9_lead: These are the divisions in charge of the matters raised on this page. The surest way to test our review is to ask the responsible division directly. Every entry is copied from what the city or the prefecture publishes (as of September 2026).
rev_s9_note: The department names are left in Japanese: that is what you will need to show at the counter or read out on the phone. The main switchboards are 0568-72-2101 for Komaki City Hall and 052-961-2111 for the Aichi Prefectural Government. Names and numbers can change when the offices are reorganized. National divisions are listed on Nationwide Trends. This site has no connection with any of these offices, and you do not need to mention it when you contact them.

rev_stance: ⚠️ This page contains this site’s own review and proposals. They are not the position of Komaki City or its Board of Education. Anything marked 【Fact】 comes from published material and is sourced, while anything marked 🔎 review or 💡 proposal is this site’s own thinking. Please read the two separately. Views for and against the plan are on Voices, and the national picture and standards are on Nationwide.
rev_stance_general: Note that the 🔎 reviews and 💡 proposals reason from general grounds — how the rules work and what other places have done — on top of the published material. This site has no inside information about the district.
rev_sum1: The plan’s numbers: the reorganization responds to the forecast that by 2033 every grade will have just one class (the numbers behind this review).
rev_sum2: 🔎 Key findings: from three angles — the plan itself (1–5), quality of education (6–8) and the number of children (9–10) — we set out in 10 points what the published materials do and do not show (key findings).
rev_sum3: 💡 Key proposals: five for protecting and raising the quality of education and five for increasing the number of children in the east (key proposals). Every item has a “More” link to its evidence.
rev_sum4: How to check: what we could not confirm, and the departments you can ask, are listed at the end (what we could not confirm · who to contact).
